problem.heading: India runs on hundreds of disconnected government apps and portals.
body: A citizen who wants to register a birth, claim a pension, or check a land record doesn't deal with one government. They deal with dozens — each with its own app, its own login, its own language, and its own idea of how a form should work.
Services exist, but finding the real one — not a lookalike, not a middleman — takes confidence, data, and patience that the people who need help most often don't have. The maze itself is the barrier.
Saathi asks a simpler question: what if there were just one door?
problem.appsLabel: A few of the apps a citizen is expected to juggle
problem.quote: मुझे पता है कि सब online है, but मुझे ये नहीं पता कि कौन सा online असली है.
problem.quoteTranslation: I know everything's online — I just don't know which 'online' is the real one.

reflection.heading: What I'd do next.
body: Scoped out for now: real Aadhaar and payments, live speech recognition in every language, and an offline-first data layer.
Next, I'd pressure-test the voice flows with low-literacy users, put every language in front of native reviewers — the 19 machine-assisted ones first.
reflection.aboutBody: I'm a product designer working on civic and consumer products. Saathi is a self-initiated exploration of what dignified, inclusive government software could feel like.

research.heading: I talked to citizens across India.
research.body: Over several weeks I spoke with people in cities, small towns and villages about the last time they dealt with a government service. The same three frictions surfaced again and again: language, trust, and simply not knowing where to start.

personas.name: Rakesh

personas.name: Sunita

personas.name: Vikram
personas.line: Wants it read aloud, in Tamil, without rushing.

personas.name: Ananya

umang.heading: India already built one app. Here's what Saathi does differently.
umang.intro: UMANG is the government's own unified app — thousands of services in one place. It proved aggregation is possible. Saathi starts where UMANG stops: not 'how many services fit', but 'how does it feel for a real person to use one'.

rows.umang: A directory of departments and services — you must already know the exact name.
rows.saathi: Life moments, needs and entitlements — you start from your situation, not a department.

rows.umang: 13 languages, but most forms still fall back to English.
rows.saathi: Vernacular-first, voice on every field, and the whole UI swaps script in 200ms.

rows.umang: You search — nothing tells you what you're actually owed.
rows.saathi: Profile-based scheme cards with a transparent 'why you qualify'.

rows.umang: Official, but visually dense and utilitarian.
rows.saathi: Calm authority — verification and status surfaced in the first five seconds.

rows.umang: Largely on your own once you submit.
rows.saathi: A status timeline with named officers, and family-proxy as a first-class action.

rows.umang: Standard forms; little for low-literacy or low-vision users.
rows.saathi: Slow mode, larger text, read-aloud and offline-first — on by default.

umang.note: UMANG is a real, large-scale product serving millions. This comparison is about design philosophy — not a critique of its engineering or reach.

cs.title: Designing one door to every government service
cs.lede: A UI/UX case study on Saathi — a multilingual, voice-first citizen app with an assistant that asks before it acts, designed for Viksit Bharat @2047.

meta.label: Role
meta.value: Product designer — research, UX, UI, motion, prototype

meta.label: Languages
meta.value: 23 languages — all 22 of the Eighth Schedule, plus English

meta.label: Deliverables
meta.value: Research, design system, working prototype, website

overview.heading: One door, not hundreds.
body: India has built the rails of a digital state — identity, payments, documents and language technology at a scale no other country has attempted. What it doesn't yet have is a front door that feels made for the person standing in front of it.

Saathi reorganises government services around what happens in a citizen's life, speaks their language, and adds an assistant that can prepare an application, show its plan, ask for consent and hand back proof.

outcomes.label: government processes modelled on their real portals
languages — English and every one of the 22 in the Eighth Schedule
onboarding steps, including consent under the DPDP Act
assistant that never submits without your yes

ai.heading: An assistant that acts — and asks first.
body: Most government chatbots answer questions. The people we designed for don't need more answers; they need the thing done. So Saathi AI is designed as an agent: it plans, uses official services and produces an outcome.
Acting on someone's behalf with their identity and money raises the bar for trust. Every pattern below exists to keep the citizen in control.

patterns.title: Plan card
patterns.body: Before doing anything, Saathi lists its steps and the official service behind each one. The plan updates live as steps complete.

patterns.title: Tool steps
patterns.body: Each action — fetching a record from DigiLocker, checking eligibility — appears as a short, verifiable line with its source.

patterns.title: Consent gate
patterns.body: Nothing is submitted, paid or shared until the citizen approves a card that names the data, the recipient and how long access lasts.

patterns.title: Outcome
patterns.body: Every mission ends in something real: an application in Track, a paid receipt, a switched language — with a reference number.

failures.title: Didn't understand
failures.body: Offer three likely requests in plain words, and the option to speak to a person.

failures.title: Not eligible
failures.body: Say so plainly, explain which rule applies, and suggest what the person may qualify for instead.

failures.title: Service unavailable
failures.body: Keep the prepared application as a draft and say when to retry. Never lose what someone has entered.

failures.title: Needs a human
failures.body: Hand over to the nearest Common Service Centre or a helpline, with the context already filled in.

principles: Asks before it acts on identity, money or data
Shows its reasoning for every eligibility claim
A person is always one tap away
Scripted and reviewable — no hidden prompts deciding outcomes
ai.note: In this prototype the assistant is pre-scripted, not a live language model — so every answer it gives can be reviewed before it reaches a citizen.

structure.heading: Five tabs. The assistant in the middle.
structure.body: Version one had an Apply tab — but a bare Apply tab asks “apply for what?”. The centre of Saathi 2.0 is the assistant: tell it what you need, in any words, and it routes you. Every one of the 42 flows is still reachable from Explore, detail screens and Home.

accessibility.contrastBody: Contrast ratios are computed from the design tokens in code and checked in automated tests against WCAG 2.1 AA.

system.heading: Bharat Precision.
system.body: A design system calm enough to trust with a pension and precise enough to feel world-class — on a pure white base, with colour reserved for meaning.

colours.name: Saffron
colours.use: Attention and highlights, never body text

system.typeBody: Geist for Latin, Anek for Indic headlines (by Ek Type, an Indian foundry) and Noto Sans for Indic body text at a 1.8 line height, as UX4G recommends.
system.imageryBody: No stock photos and no maps. Kolam linework for texture, guilloche security print for anything official.
system.motionBody: Interface motion stays under 300 milliseconds and can always be interrupted. Storytelling motion breathes. Everything becomes a gentle fade for people who prefer reduced motion.

success.heading: How we'd know it works.
success.body: These are design targets for a pilot, not results. They are here so the design can be judged against something measurable.
